processing: Standard Wenshan Bao Zhong leaf (light oxidation, twisted strips) given a medium roast in ovens or over charcoal, often in several passes, which turns the florals into chestnut and toast; heavier versions are re-roasted over the years and sold as aged Bao Zhong.
harvest_season: Spring and winter leaf, roasted in the months after harvest; much of it is the previous year's leaf given a second life.
appearance_dry: Twisted dark-brown strips with a dull surface and a nutty, toasty smell.
appearance_wet: Brown-olive leaves, still whole and twisted, softer and darker than the green style.
taste_profile: Roasted chestnut and toast first, then warm honey and a faded orchid note on a smoother, rounder body than green Bao Zhong, with a gentle toasty finish and no bitterness.

brewing.notes: Hotter water than the green style, just off the boil; a clay pot does it no harm. Six or seven steeps, with the roast receding and the sweetness growing.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest and roast year, usually from the previous year's spring or winter leaf, with the roast level ranging from a light toasting to something close to charcoal Dong Ding; competition Bao Zhong is the green style, so graded packs of this are rare. Aged lots re-roasted over the years are sold by claimed decade, and ten- to thirty-year-old Pinglin Bao Zhong is a quiet local speciality.
description:
Roasted Bao Zhong, called shu xiang ('ripe aroma') or bei huo ('fired') Bao Zhong in Pinglin, is the traditional way of finishing Wenshan's strip-shaped oolong before the fashion for green, unroasted tea took over. The twisted, lightly oxidised leaf is given a medium roast in several passes, which turns the lily florals into chestnut and warm honey and gives the tea a shelf life the green style never has.

Historically most Bao Zhong was roasted because it was shipped to Southeast Asia and had to survive the journey; today it is a minority product, made by older Pinglin and Shiding makers for drinkers who find the green style too delicate, and used to give last year's unsold leaf a second life. A heavier roast repeated over the years turns it into aged Bao Zhong, a quiet local speciality.

The cup is roasted chestnut and toast first, then honey and a faded orchid note, on a smoother, rounder body than the green style, with a gentle toasty finish and no bitterness. It takes hotter water than fresh Bao Zhong, just off the boil, and a clay pot does it no harm; six or seven steeps, with the roast receding and the sweetness growing.

It is sold by harvest and roast year, usually from the previous year's spring or winter leaf, and the roast level is worth asking about because it ranges from a light toasting to something close to charcoal Dong Ding. Competition Bao Zhong is the green style, so you will rarely find graded packs of this; buy from a Pinglin maker directly or from a shop that can say who roasted it. Aged lots are sold by claimed decade.

It is a good tea for people who like Hong Shui or roasted Dong Ding but want something lighter in the hand and quicker to brew.
history: Roasted Bao Zhong is the strip-shaped oolong of Pinglin and Shiding finished with a real roast, unlike the green style that dominates today. Makers treat it as an older way of handling this leaf, and it also serves to refresh tea left from an earlier harvest. Little is documented in detail about how the style developed or how widely it is still made.
